question: Why does speed matter most among the complexities of cloud monitoring?
option_a: Because cloud providers delete telemetry after a few minutes, so it must be read at once
option_b: Because attacks on cloud systems are often scripted, so data can be stolen or exposed within seconds or minutes of the first break-in
option_c: Because the management plane throttles slow queries, making delayed analysis impossible
option_d: Because the shared-responsibility model requires the customer to report incidents to the provider in real time

question: What does the Target 2013 case illustrate about monitoring?
option_a: Anomaly detection produces too many false positives to be useful in retail
option_b: Third-party contractors should never be given network access
option_c: Detection is half the task: an alert nobody responds to is no better than no alert
option_d: Point-of-sale systems cannot be monitored with management plane logs

question: Which statement correctly distinguishes an IDS from an IPS?
option_a: An IDS sits inline and blocks malicious traffic; an IPS observes a copy and alerts
option_b: An IDS observes a copy of the traffic out-of-band and raises alerts; an IPS sits inline and can block traffic, at the risk of blocking a real user on a false positive
option_c: An IDS works only by signature; an IPS works only by anomaly
option_d: An IDS is a cloud service; an IPS is always a physical appliance

question: In one or two sentences: what is the cascade-and-filter pattern, and which two purposes does it serve?
accepted_answers: a sequence of detection mechanisms, each narrowing the data further; filters from broadly suspicious toward known attack patterns to a confirmed alert; turns many events into few alerts and manages cost; most raw logs stay cheaply in place, only pertinent alerts go to the security team

question: Name two of the key indicators or detectors the Guidance says to watch closely on the management plane and identity systems.
accepted_answers: unauthorised API calls; management console logins without MFA; any IAM policy change; any use of the root account; unusual IAM or network security activity, especially in unused regions

question: Why does the simple monitoring loop - poll every instance, alert if one fails to respond - not fit cloud-native applications?
option_a: Cloud providers forbid polling because it consumes API quota
option_b: Cloud-native instances start and stop all the time under the orchestrator's control, so a disappearing instance is not by itself a sign of trouble
option_c: The loop is too fast: thirty seconds is shorter than the fast path requires
option_d: Cloud-native applications run a known number of instances in known places, so polling is redundant

question: Building on the "The canary token" exercise: the Nextcloud team's analysts are drowning in alerts, most of them false positives, and worry they would miss a real intrusion. Propose a design that adds one canary to the deployment and routes its alerts appropriately: say what the canary is, why any access to it is almost certainly malicious, whether its alert belongs on the fast path or the slow path and why, and name one other key indicator from this chapter you would put on the same path. Justify each choice with a concept from this chapter.
sample_answer: A decoy such as a fake admin_passwords.txt file or an unused decoy user account in Nextcloud; since no legitimate process ever touches it, any interaction indicates an attempted or actual breach, giving almost no false positives. Its alert belongs on the fast path, because a triggered canary is high-risk activity and the slow path's delay of up to fifteen minutes is too long; fast-path events become alerts almost at once. On the same path: another key indicator such as management console logins without MFA, an IAM policy change, root account use, or impossible-travel logins. Grading: full credit needs a plausible canary, the no-legitimate-access argument, fast path with the timeliness justification, and one correct key indicator; partial credit for three of the four.
